title: 12 — Concurrency, Async & Parallelism
html:
12 — Concurrency, Async & Parallelism

The distinction that clears up 80% of the confusion: Concurrency = dealing with many things at once (structure). Parallelism = doing many things at once (execution). Asynchrony = not blocking while waiting (efficiency). A single-core machine can be concurrent and asynchronous but never parallel.

1. The mental model

CPU-bound work           →  parallelism  →  more cores help  →  Parallel.For, PLINQ, multiprocessing
I/O-bound work           →  asynchrony   →  more threads DON'T help  →  async/await, asyncio
Both, at scale           →  a pipeline: async I/O feeding a bounded parallel compute stage

flowchart LR
    subgraph Sync["Synchronous I/O — 1 thread per request"]
        T1["Thread: request → [BLOCKED 200ms waiting on DB] → respond"]
    end
    subgraph Async["Asynchronous I/O — thread returned to the pool"]
        T2["Thread: request → await → (thread serves other requests) → continuation → respond"]
    end

The economics: a thread costs ~1 MB of stack plus scheduler overhead. At 10,000 concurrent requests, synchronous I/O needs 10,000 threads (~10 GB, unusable). Async needs a handful — the requests are waiting, not working, and waiting doesn't require a thread.

⚠️ async does not make anything faster. A single request takes the same wall-clock time. It increases throughput and scalability by not wasting threads. Saying "we made it async so it's faster" in an interview is a red flag.

2. .NET async/await

2.1 What the compiler actually does

async methods are compiled into a state machine. await splits the method at each suspension point; the remainder becomes a continuation scheduled when the awaited operation completes.

public async Task<Quote> GetQuoteAsync(string symbol, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var response = await _http.GetAsync($"/quotes/{symbol}", ct);   // ← state machine suspends here
    response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
    return await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<Quote>(ct)      // ← and here
           ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("Empty quote payload.");
}

Key facts:

  • No thread is used while awaiting real I/O. The I/O completion port / epoll notification resumes it.
  • Task is a promise of a future result, not a thread.
  • An async method runs synchronously until the first await that actually suspends. If the awaited task is already complete, it continues on the same thread with no context switch.
  • ValueTask<T> avoids the Task allocation when the result is usually already available (cache hits, buffered reads). ⚠️ It can only be awaited once and must not be stored — use Task for public APIs unless you've measured the allocation as a problem.

2.2 The rules

Rule Why
Async all the way down A single sync-over-async bridge reintroduces thread blocking and can deadlock
Never .Result, .Wait(), .GetAwaiter().GetResult() Blocks a thread; deadlocks in any context with a synchronization context
Accept and propagate CancellationToken on every public async API Otherwise nothing can be cancelled or timed out
ConfigureAwait(false) in libraries Avoids capturing a synchronization context you don't need. ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext, so app code doesn't need it
Don't async void Except for event handlers. Exceptions in async void cannot be caught — they crash the process
Return Task directly when there's no work after the await public Task<X> Get() => _inner.GetAsync(); avoids a state machine — but not inside using/try blocks, where you need await for correct scoping
Task.WhenAll for independent work Sequential awaits serialise operations that could overlap 
// ❌ Serial: 3 × 200 ms = 600 ms
var a = await GetPortfolioAsync(id, ct);
var b = await GetBenchmarkAsync(id, ct);
var c = await GetPricesAsync(id, ct);

// ✔ Concurrent: ~200 ms
var portfolioTask = GetPortfolioAsync(id, ct);
var benchmarkTask = GetBenchmarkAsync(id, ct);
var pricesTask    = GetPricesAsync(id, ct);
await Task.WhenAll(portfolioTask, benchmarkTask, pricesTask);
var (a, b, c) = (portfolioTask.Result, benchmarkTask.Result, pricesTask.Result);  // safe: already complete

⚠️ Task.WhenAll only surfaces the first exception when awaited. To see all of them, inspect whenAllTask.Exception (an AggregateException). And note the tasks all start when created, not when awaited — if you need to limit concurrency, don't start them all at once (§2.5).

2.3 Deadlock: the classic

// In a UI app or legacy ASP.NET (with a SynchronizationContext), this deadlocks:
public string GetData() => GetDataAsync().Result;

private async Task<string> GetDataAsync()
{
    await _http.GetStringAsync(url);   // captures the context; wants to resume ON the UI thread
    return "done";                      // ...which is blocked inside .Result. Deadlock.
}

Fix: don't block. Make the caller async. ConfigureAwait(false) avoids this particular deadlock but treats the symptom — the real problem is the sync-over-async bridge, which also burns a thread.

2.4 Thread-pool starvation — the #1 production async bug

Symptom: the app becomes slow under load, request latency climbs into seconds, CPU is low, and it partially recovers after a while. Looks like a network problem; isn't.

Cause: threads blocked on sync-over-async (or on a lock, or on Thread.Sleep) inside pool threads. The pool injects new threads slowly (~1–2 per second by default), so the queue grows faster than it drains.

Diagnosis:

dotnet-counters monitor -p <pid> System.Runtime
# watch: ThreadPool Thread Count climbing, ThreadPool Queue Length > 0 and growing

Fixes: eliminate every .Result/.Wait(); use SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync() not Wait(); use await Task.Delay() not Thread.Sleep(); never call synchronous I/O APIs in a request path. As a stopgap only: ThreadPool.SetMinThreads.

2.5 Bounded concurrency

// Process 10,000 items with at most 8 in flight
var throttle = new SemaphoreSlim(8);
var tasks = items.Select(async item =>
{
    await throttle.WaitAsync(ct);
    try { return await ProcessAsync(item, ct); }
    finally { throttle.Release(); }
});
var results = await Task.WhenAll(tasks);

// .NET 6+: cleaner, with built-in cancellation and parallelism control
await Parallel.ForEachAsync(items,
    new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 8, CancellationToken = ct },
    async (item, token) => await ProcessAsync(item, token));

⚠️ Unbounded fan-out is a self-inflicted DDoS. Task.WhenAll(items.Select(ProcessAsync)) over 50,000 items will open 50,000 connections, exhaust the pool, and take down the downstream service. Always bound it.

2.6 Cancellation

public async Task<Report> BuildAsync(ReportRequest request, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // Combine the caller's token with a local timeout
    using var timeout = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(ct);
    timeout.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30));

    var data = await _repository.LoadAsync(request.Id, timeout.Token);

    foreach (var section in request.Sections)
    {
        timeout.Token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();     // check in CPU-bound loops
        Render(section, data);
    }
    return new Report(...);
}
  • Cancellation is cooperative — nothing is forcibly aborted. Code that ignores the token can't be cancelled.
  • OperationCanceledException is expected control flow on cancellation; don't log it as an error.
  • In ASP.NET Core, HttpContext.RequestAborted fires when the client disconnects — accept CancellationToken in your actions and you get free abandonment of work nobody is waiting for.

2.7 IAsyncEnumerable for streaming

public async IAsyncEnumerable<Trade> StreamTradesAsync(
    DateOnly from, [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)
{
    await using var conn = await _factory.OpenAsync(ct);
    await using var reader = await conn.ExecuteReaderAsync(Sql.TradesSince, new { from }, ct);
    while (await reader.ReadAsync(ct))
        yield return Map(reader);          // constant memory over millions of rows
}

await foreach (var trade in StreamTradesAsync(from, ct))
    await sink.WriteAsync(trade, ct);

Use for large result sets, paged APIs, and server-sent streams — anywhere materialising the whole list would blow memory.

2.8 Background work

// ❌ Fire-and-forget: exceptions are lost, work is killed on shutdown
_ = SendEmailAsync(user);

// ✔ Producer/consumer with a hosted service
public sealed class EmailQueue
{
    private readonly Channel<EmailMessage> _channel =
        Channel.CreateBounded<EmailMessage>(new BoundedChannelOptions(1000)
        {
            FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait     // backpressure onto the producer
        });

    public ValueTask EnqueueAsync(EmailMessage m, CancellationToken ct) =>
        _channel.Writer.WriteAsync(m, ct);

    public IAsyncEnumerable<EmailMessage> ReadAllAsync(CancellationToken ct) =>
        _channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync(ct);
}

public sealed class EmailWorker(EmailQueue queue, IEmailSender sender, ILogger<EmailWorker> log)
    : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        await foreach (var message in queue.ReadAllAsync(stoppingToken))
        {
            try { await sender.SendAsync(message, stoppingToken); }
            catch (Exception ex) { log.LogError(ex, "Failed to send email to {Recipient}", message.To); }
        }
    }
}

⚠️ In-process queues lose work on restart. For anything that must not be lost, use a durable queue (file 14). Channel<T> is the right tool for in-process pipelines and load-shaping, not for durability.

3. Parallelism for CPU-bound work

// Data parallelism
Parallel.For(0, matrix.Rows, new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = Environment.ProcessorCount },
             row => ComputeRow(matrix, row));

// PLINQ — good for pure transforms; measure, it isn't always faster
var results = source.AsParallel()
                    .WithDegreeOfParallelism(8)
                    .Select(Expensive)
                    .ToArray();

When parallelism helps: genuinely CPU-bound work, items are independent, per-item work is large enough (> ~10 µs) to dwarf the partitioning overhead, and the data fits comfortably in memory.

Amdahl's law: speedup ≤ 1 / (S + P/N), where S is the serial fraction. A 10% serial fraction caps you at 10× no matter how many cores. Locks, shared counters, and logging in the loop are all serial fractions.

⚠️ False sharing: two threads writing to different variables that share a 64-byte cache line cause constant cache-line ping-pong; throughput can be worse than single-threaded. Fix: pad to cache-line boundaries, or accumulate into thread-local state and combine at the end (Parallel.For has an overload for exactly this).

⚠️ Don't mix Parallel.For with async work. Parallel.For(… async …) produces async void lambdas — fire-and-forget, no waiting, exceptions lost. Use Parallel.ForEachAsync.

4. Synchronisation primitives (.NET)

Primitive Scope Async? Use
lock / Monitor / System.Threading.Lock (.NET 9) In-process ✘ Short critical sections. Default choice
SemaphoreSlim In-process (or named: cross-process) ✔ WaitAsync Throttling, async-safe mutual exclusion
Mutex Cross-process ✘ Single-instance app, cross-process locking
ReaderWriterLockSlim In-process ✘ Read-heavy, write-rare (measure — often a plain lock wins)
Interlocked In-process n/a Atomic counters, CAS loops. Fastest
ConcurrentDictionary/Queue/Bag In-process n/a Lock-free-ish collections
Channel<T> In-process ✔ Producer/consumer — avoids locks entirely
Barrier, CountdownEvent In-process partial Phase coordination
Lazy<T> In-process n/a Thread-safe one-time initialisation
Distributed lock (Redis/DB/Blob lease) Cross-machine ✔ Cross-node coordination — see file 11 §5.2 caveats 
// ❌ Never lock on these: external code can lock the same instance and deadlock you
lock (this) { }
lock (typeof(Foo)) { }
lock ("mykey") { }                 // string interning makes this global!

// ✔
private readonly Lock _gate = new();          // .NET 9+; `private readonly object _gate = new();` before
lock (_gate) { /* short, no I/O, no await (you can't await inside lock anyway) */ }

// ✔ Async-safe mutual exclusion
private readonly SemaphoreSlim _gate = new(1, 1);
await _gate.WaitAsync(ct);
try { await DoAsync(ct); } finally { _gate.Release(); }

Rules for locks:

  1. Hold for as short a time as possible; never do I/O or call unknown code inside a lock.
  2. Acquire multiple locks in a globally consistent order (prevents deadlock).
  3. Never await inside lock — the compiler forbids it, and that's a hint that you want SemaphoreSlim.
  4. Prefer not sharing state over locking it well.

5. The memory model — why "it works on my machine" happens

Both the compiler/JIT and the CPU may reorder operations. Without synchronisation, one thread's writes are not guaranteed to be visible to another in program order.

// ❌ Classic broken flag: the loop may never see the update (the JIT can hoist the read)
private bool _stop;                       // no volatile, no lock
void Worker() { while (!_stop) { DoWork(); } }
void Stop()   { _stop = true; }

// ✔ Options, in order of preference
private volatile bool _stop;                      // acquire/release semantics on this field
// or
private readonly CancellationTokenSource _cts = new();   // the idiomatic .NET answer
Tool Guarantee
volatile Prevents certain reorderings around this field; does not make compound operations atomic (_count++ is still a race)
Interlocked.* Atomic read-modify-write + full fence
lock Mutual exclusion + full memory barrier on entry and exit
Volatile.Read/Write Explicit acquire/release for a single access

Practical guidance: don't reason about the memory model if you can avoid it. Use lock, Interlocked, concurrent collections, or immutability. Lock-free algorithms are a specialist skill and the failure mode is a rare, undebuggable production corruption.

Atomicity note: reads/writes of types ≤ pointer size (int, bool, references) are atomic in .NET; long/double on 32-bit and structs larger than a word are not — a torn read is possible.

6. Common concurrency bugs

Bug Example Detection Fix
Race condition if (!dict.ContainsKey(k)) dict.Add(k, v); Intermittent, load-dependent TryAdd, GetOrAdd, or lock the whole check-and-act
Deadlock Two locks in opposite orders Hangs; dump shows threads waiting Consistent lock ordering; timeouts; fewer locks
Livelock Two threads retry forever, politely yielding High CPU, no progress Randomised backoff
Starvation A low-priority thread never runs Unfair latency distribution Fair queueing
Lost update Read-modify-write without atomicity Wrong totals Interlocked, atomic SQL, optimistic concurrency
Thread-pool starvation Sync-over-async Low CPU, high latency, growing queue §2.4
Captive dependency Scoped DbContext in a singleton Random InvalidOperationException, cross-request bleed IServiceScopeFactory
Non-thread-safe reuse Sharing DbContext, HttpContext, Random, or StringBuilder across threads Corrupt state, weird exceptions Per-thread instances; Random.Shared (.NET 6+)
Async void async void handler throws Process crash, no stack Return Task; wrap handlers in try/catch
Unobserved task exception Fire-and-forget failure Silent Await, or attach a continuation that logs
Double-checked locking done wrong Missing volatile on the field Rare torn initialisation Use Lazy<T> 
// ✔ Correct one-time init — don't hand-roll double-checked locking
private readonly Lazy<ExpensiveThing> _thing =
    new(() => new ExpensiveThing(), LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication);

Testing concurrency: deterministic tests are hard. What works: stress loops (run 10,000 iterations across N threads and assert an invariant), injecting delays at suspicious points, ConcurrentQueue assertions on ordering, and making the code single-threaded by design (a Channel<T> with one consumer removes the whole class of bug).

7. Python concurrency

7.1 The GIL, precisely

CPython's Global Interpreter Lock allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. Consequences:

  • Threads do NOT give CPU parallelism for pure Python code.
  • Threads DO help for I/O — the GIL is released during blocking I/O (sockets, files) and inside C extensions that release it (NumPy, Polars, pandas ops, hashlib).
  • CPU-bound Python parallelism requires multiprocessing (separate interpreters, separate memory, IPC cost) or offloading to native code.
  • Python 3.13+ has an experimental free-threaded build (PEP 703) removing the GIL; not yet the default and ecosystem support is partial.
Workload Tool
I/O-bound, many connections asyncio (best), or ThreadPoolExecutor
I/O-bound, simple/blocking libraries ThreadPoolExecutor
CPU-bound, pure Python ProcessPoolExecutor / multiprocessing
CPU-bound, array/dataframe work NumPy/Polars/DuckDB — they release the GIL and parallelise internally. This is almost always the right answer
Distributed Dask, Ray, Spark

7.2 asyncio

import asyncio
import httpx

async def fetch_quote(client: httpx.AsyncClient, symbol: str) -> dict:
    response = await client.get(f"/quotes/{symbol}", timeout=5.0)
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()

async def fetch_all(symbols: list[str], concurrency: int = 10) -> list[dict]:
    limiter = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency)          # bound concurrency, same rule as .NET

    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url="https://api.example.com") as client:
        async def guarded(symbol: str) -> dict:
            async with limiter:
                return await fetch_quote(client, symbol)

        return await asyncio.gather(*(guarded(s) for s in symbols))

Rules:

  • ⚠️ One blocking call poisons the entire event loop. time.sleep(), requests.get(), a sync DB driver, or a heavy CPU loop inside a coroutine blocks every other task. Use await asyncio.sleep(), httpx/aiohttp, async drivers — or push the blocking call to asyncio.to_thread(fn, *args).
  • Use asyncio.TaskGroup (3.11+) over bare gather — structured concurrency with proper cancellation and exception propagation.
  • asyncio.timeout() (3.11+) for deadlines.
  • Never mix sync and async versions of the same library in one path.
# Structured concurrency — if any task fails, the others are cancelled cleanly
async def load_portfolio(pid: str) -> Portfolio:
    async with asyncio.timeout(10):
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            holdings = tg.create_task(fetch_holdings(pid))
            prices   = tg.create_task(fetch_prices(pid))
            meta     = tg.create_task(fetch_metadata(pid))
    return build(holdings.result(), prices.result(), meta.result())

7.3 multiprocessing

from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

def score_chunk(chunk: list[Record]) -> list[float]:
    return [expensive_pure_python(r) for r in chunk]

with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=8) as pool:
    results = list(pool.map(score_chunk, chunks))

⚠️ Arguments and results are pickled — a large DataFrame per task can cost more in serialisation than the computation saves. Prefer chunking coarse, returning small results, or using shared memory (multiprocessing.shared_memory) / Arrow IPC.

8. JavaScript / TypeScript concurrency (for the Angular side)

Single-threaded event loop + microtask queue.

Call stack empties
  → drain ALL microtasks (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask)
  → run ONE macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, UI event)
  → repeat

Consequences: a Promise.resolve().then() chain runs before a setTimeout(fn, 0); a long synchronous loop freezes the UI including rendering and input, because there is nowhere else to run.

Tools:

  • async/await over promises; Promise.all (fail-fast), Promise.allSettled (collect all outcomes), Promise.race (timeouts).
  • Web Workers for genuine CPU parallelism (separate thread, message-passing, no DOM access). Use for parsing large payloads, crypto, image processing.
  • RxJS for streams of events with cancellation, backpressure-ish operators, and composition — see file 17 for operator selection.
  • AbortController for cancelling fetch.
// Bounded concurrency in TS, same principle as everywhere else
async function mapWithConcurrency<T, R>(
  items: readonly T[],
  limit: number,
  fn: (item: T) => Promise<R>,
): Promise<R[]> {
  const results: R[] = new Array(items.length);
  let cursor = 0;

  const workers = Array.from({ length: Math.min(limit, items.length) }, async () => {
    while (cursor < items.length) {
      const index = cursor++;
      results[index] = await fn(items[index]);
    }
  });

  await Promise.all(workers);
  return results;
}

9. Distributed concurrency

Everything above assumes one process. Across machines you additionally lose: shared memory, a common clock, and the ability to distinguish "slow" from "dead".

Problem Approach
Mutual exclusion across nodes Database row lock / advisory lock; blob lease; ZooKeeper/etcd. Redis lock only with fencing tokens and non-critical semantics
Leader election Raft-backed store (etcd/Consul), Kubernetes lease, or a DB row with a TTL
Idempotency Idempotency keys + a uniqueness constraint. The only reliable exactly-once mechanism
Ordering Per-partition sequence numbers; logical clocks. Never wall-clock timestamps across machines
Consistency Quorums (W+R>N), or a single writer per partition
Coordination-free CRDTs, append-only logs, partitioning so that each key has one owner

Fencing tokens — the fix for the "lock holder was paused by GC and woke up thinking it still held the lock" problem:

Lock service returns a monotonically increasing token with the lock.
Every write to the protected resource carries the token.
The resource rejects any write with a token lower than the highest it has seen.

Without this, no lease-based distributed lock is safe under arbitrary process pauses.

Best strategy: design so you don't need distributed mutual exclusion. Partition the work so each key is owned by exactly one consumer (Kafka partitions, consistent hashing), and make operations idempotent.

10. Debugging concurrency in production

Symptom Likely cause Tool
High latency, low CPU Thread-pool starvation, lock contention, slow I/O dotnet-counters (queue length), dotnet-stack, dump analysis
High CPU, no progress Spin-waiting, livelock, busy loop dotnet-trace, perf top
Process hangs Deadlock Dump → !syncblk/parallel stacks in WinDbg/dotnet-dump
Intermittent wrong data Race condition Code review of check-then-act patterns; stress test
Memory growth Unbounded queue/channel, leaked timers/subscriptions Heap dump, dotnet-gcdump
Occasional crash, no stack async void exception Search the codebase for async void 
dotnet-counters monitor -p <pid> System.Runtime
dotnet-dump collect -p <pid>
dotnet-stack report -p <pid>        # what every thread is doing, right now

11. Checklist & interview angles

Concurrency review checklist

  • No .Result, .Wait(), .GetAwaiter().GetResult() anywhere in a request path
  • No async void except event handlers
  • CancellationToken accepted and propagated through every async layer
  • Every fan-out is bounded (SemaphoreSlim / MaxDegreeOfParallelism)
  • Shared mutable state is either eliminated, immutable, or protected — and the protection is documented
  • Locks: private lock objects, consistent order, no I/O held
  • Background work is durable if it must not be lost
  • DI lifetimes: no scoped services captured by singletons
  • Non-thread-safe types (DbContext, Random pre-.NET 6, StringBuilder) are not shared
  • Timeouts on every await that can hang
  • Load-tested at target concurrency, watching thread count and queue length

🔍 Interview angles

  • Concurrency vs parallelism vs asynchrony? Structure vs simultaneous execution vs non-blocking waiting. Async improves throughput, not single-request latency.
  • Why does async improve scalability? It returns the thread to the pool during I/O waits, so a small pool serves many in-flight requests.
  • What is thread-pool starvation and how do you diagnose it? Blocked pool threads + slow injection → growing queue, high latency, low CPU. Diagnose with counters; fix by removing blocking.
  • Why does .Result deadlock in some apps but not ASP.NET Core? ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext to capture, so the continuation can run on any pool thread. It still wastes a thread.
  • How would you limit concurrent calls to a flaky downstream? SemaphoreSlim bulkhead + timeout + circuit breaker.
  • Explain the GIL. One thread executes Python bytecode at a time; released during I/O and in native extensions; use processes or native libraries for CPU parallelism.
  • How do you make an operation idempotent in a distributed system? Client-supplied idempotency key + a unique constraint at the storage layer; the second attempt returns the first result rather than re-executing.
  • Is a Redis lock safe? Not for correctness-critical work without fencing tokens; process pauses and clock drift break the mutual-exclusion argument.
